messages.subject: Understanding goodness-of-fit results
messages.subject_clean: Understanding goodness-of-fit results
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

As I specified in a previous message, I am fairly new to the unmarked package and am trying to work through some problems.

I have a dataset that includes double observer data for a single date/ season. The data looks like this:
Species site ob1 ob2 ob1ID ob2ID
AMCR    A     1     1        Jane    John
AMCR    B      0     1       Jane    John
 . . . .
AMCR   Y       1    1          Fred    Barbara
AMCR   Z       0    0          Fred    Barbara

I have created global models for the individual species in the dataset using the occu() function, and have used the mb.gof.test() function

from the AICcmodavg package to perform goodness-of-fit tests. However, for a fair number of the species, the c-hat is greater than 4.

For example, for AMCR, the results are

   Cohort Observed Expected Chi-square
00      0      146   133.39       1.19
01      0       25    39.79       5.50
10      0       20    30.42       3.57
11      0       63    50.40       3.15

The results suggest that (1,1) and (0,0) occurs more often than expected, with (1,0) and (0,1) underrepresented. But the site data really aren't independent and it isn't unexpected that AMCR, if heard by one observer, would be heard by both observers. Since the c-hat is above 1 (8.2), the results suggest the data is overdispersed. In the MacKenzie and Bailey paper from 2004, an example is given where two sites are situated too close together and thus there is overcounting. In the current example, there is clearly overcounting!

I guess what I am asking is (1) using the mb.gof.test the appropriate way to analyze the dataset I have, and if not, what would be a better way?

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Understanding goodness-of-fit results
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Understanding goodness-of-fit results
messages.body_plain:
Hi Wade,

For a species that is easy to detect, it is more likely that both
observers will detect it during the same period. Are these two
observers independent and sampling simultaneously at the same site? Or
are they sampling at different times?

Some things that may help:
-add better covariates on detection and/or occupancy
-change the model (e.g., perhaps time to detection)
-change the data (e.g., work on guilds instead of species, exclude
species)

You indicate in your message that "the site data really aren't
independent". Do you mean that sites are close to one another and the
same individual can be detected at different sites? If there is a
spatial structure in your collection of sites (nested in region or
along a transect), then you could incorporate this structure in the
model.

Regardless, a c-hat of 8.2 indicates that you can't continue the
analysis with the current model for a given species (overdispersion is
much too high). Also be aware that although some species will be
amenable to a single species occupancy analysis, you cannot expect the
model to fit for every species (some species will too rare or common).
A multispecies model would be another option and could accommodate rare
or common species, although the approach would be outside of unmarked
(AHM1 book by Marc Kéry and Andy Royle is a good place to start).

Good luck,

Marc
--

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

Thanks for reply.  When I wrote that the "sites really aren't independent", what I meant was that the observers were at the same site at the same time. In my limited understanding of occupancy modeling, the double observer ( two observers at the same site at the same time) and a case where a single observer went to the same site on two different occasions are modeled the same way, but do have some differences. As you stated in your reply, if a bird song is loud and close, it is more likely to be heard by both observers and thus an overabundance of (1,1) cases.

I am curios about everyone's thoughts about my solution. I "solved" my problem by randomizing the observations across each row. Since the data only has a single time (with two observers), cases can be (0,0), (1,0),(0,1), and (1,1). If (1,0) are different than (0,1), this can generate model fit errors (with c-hat above 4). However, if one randomizes across rows, the cases of (0,1) and (1,0) become roughly the same and c-hat decreases accordingly. This preserves the values (there are the same number of 0s and 1s).

I can't think of a reason why this would be a problem, but you all are smarter than I am, so just wanted to throw this out to see what people thought.

messages.subject: Removing observer effect by randomizing across rows for single observation time
messages.subject_clean: Removing observer effect by randomizing across rows for single observation time
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

In a previous post, I asked about randomizing the order of observations for a single time / double observer data set. In order to satisfy myself that this would work, I simulated some data that I am asking about in this post. The script generates three four models:

mod = null , where there are different numbers of (0,1) and (1,0) observations
mod1 = model with observer included ( ~ Observer)
mod2, which assigns observations different to the columns, and
mod4, which randomizes across rows.

All the models generate a reasonable occupancy estimate, and am wondering if I am missing something if I use mod4, which randomizes across rows. Any help would be appreciated.

Here is the code:
# First simulate some data
R = 200 # number of sites
T = 2 # number of samples
NT = 4 ## number of teams
psi = .75 ## occurrence

z <- rbinom(n = R, size = 1, prob = psi)  # Latent occurrence state

# Jane paired with John, Barb with Fred
pJane = rep(0.75,R/NT)
pJohn = rep(0.50,R/NT)
pBarb = rep(0.75,R/NT)
pFred = rep(0.50,R/NT)

pHerb = rep(0.75,R/NT)
pKaren = rep(0.50,R/NT)
pIgor = rep(0.75,R/NT)
pFran = rep(0.50,R/NT)

p1 = rbind(cbind(pJane,pJohn),
          cbind(pBarb,pFred),
          cbind(pHerb,pKaren),
          cbind(pIgor,pFran))

Jane = rep("Jane",R/NT)
John = rep("John",R/NT)
Barb = rep("Barb",R/NT)
Fred = rep("Fred",R/NT)
Herb = rep("Herb",R/NT)
Karen = rep("Karen",R/NT)
Igor = rep("Igor",R/NT)
Fran = rep("Fran",R/NT)

Observer1 = data.frame(rbind(cbind(Jane,John),
                            cbind(Barb,Fred),
                            cbind(Herb,Karen),
                            cbind(Igor,Fran)))

y1 <- matrix(NA, nrow = R, ncol = T)
# Observation process: Sample detection/nondetection observations from a Bernoulli(with p) if z=1
for (j in 1:T){
  y1[,j] <- rbinom(n = R, size = 1, prob = z * p1[,j])
}

### now just change the order
p2 = rbind(cbind(pJane,pJohn),
          cbind(pFred,pBarb),
          cbind(pHerb,pKaren),
          cbind(pFran,pIgor))

Observer2 = data.frame(rbind(cbind(Jane,John),
                            cbind(Fred,Barb),
                            cbind(Herb,Karen),
                            cbind(Fran,Igor)))

y2 <- matrix(NA, nrow = R, ncol = T)
# Observation process: Sample detection/nondetection observations from a Bernoulli(with p) if z=1
for (j in 1:T){
  y2[,j] <- rbinom(n = R, size = 1, prob = z * p2[,j])
}

### create dataset
umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y1,obsCovs = list(Observer=Observer1))
umf2 = unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y2,obsCovs = list(Observer=Observer2))

### model null
mod = occu( ~ 1 ~ 1,data=umf1)
mb.gof.test(mod)

### now add observer
mod1 = occu(~ Observer ~ 1, data=umf1)
mb.gof.test(mod1)

table(y1[,1],y1[,2])

### different order of observers
mod2 = occu( ~ 1 ~ 1,data=umf2)
mb.gof.test(mod2)

### Now simply randomize across rows

umf3 = umf1

a = umf3@y
b = a
b[b<2] = NA
for (j in 1:nrow(a)){
  b[j,] = (sample(a[j,],2))
}
table(a[,1],a[,2])
table(b[,1],b[,2])
umf3@y = b ## replace observations with randomized

mod3 = occu( ~ 1 ~ 1,data=umf3)
mb.gof.test(mod3)

table(b[,1],b[,2])

messages.subject: Understanding parameter estimates from occu() function
messages.subject_clean: Understanding parameter estimates from occu() function
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Sorry for all the posts. There are just a few things that I don't understand and haven't been able to figure out through reading the manuals, etc.

I can't figure out the scale that the se of the occu() function are on.

For example, the following code:

data <- read.csv(system.file("csv", "widewt.csv", package = "unmarked"))
y <- data[ ,2:4]
siteCovs <-  data[ ,5:7]
obsCovs <- list(date = data[ ,8:10],ivel = data[ ,11:13])
umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y, siteCovs = siteCovs, obsCovs = obsCovs)
### standardize variables
umf@siteCovs$elev <- scale(umf@siteCovs$elev)
umf@siteCovs$forest <- scale(umf@siteCovs$forest)
umf@siteCovs$length <- scale(umf@siteCovs$length)

umf@obsCovs$date <- scale(umf@obsCovs$date)
umf@obsCovs$ivel <- scale(umf@obsCovs$ivel)

### fit model. Results are on the link scale
fm <- occu(formula = ~ 1  ~ 1,data = umf)
fm
### end code

yields the following:

Call:
occu(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = umf)

Occupancy:
 Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
   -0.665 0.139 -4.77 1.82e-06

Detection:
 Estimate    SE    z  P(>|z|)
     1.32 0.174 7.61 2.82e-14

AIC: 528.987

so the occupancy parameter is -0.665. Which translates to .33 using the function
logitToProb <- function(x) { exp(x) / (1 + exp(x) ) }

However, the se (0.139) translates as 0.53, whereas if I use the backTransform function,
backTransform(fm, type = "state")

The se is listed as 0.03.

Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Occupancy estimate(s)

 Estimate     SE LinComb (Intercept)
     0.34 0.0313  -0.665           1

Transformation: logistic

Can someone explain why these are different and how I go about transform the SEs in the unmarkedfit object?

Thanks for any information.

messages.subject: Re: Understanding parameter estimates from occu() function
messages.subject_clean: Understanding parameter estimates from occu() function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Wade,

The parameters and standard errors are estimated/computed on the link scale, and backTransform uses the delta method to compute an approximation of the standard error on the probability scale. In most cases, I don't think the SE reported by backTransform or predict is of great interest. The SE (or a delta method approximation of some parameter combination) on the link scale is used to generate CI using the predict function. If you use the predict function you should get CI that look like c(plogis(-.665-(1.96*0.139)), plogis(-.665+(1.96*0.139))). Obviously, 0.34+/- 1.96*0.0313 will produce a similar interval in this case, but this calculation will always yield a symmetric interval on the probability scale that could conceivably lead to CI less than 0 or greater than 1--this is typically not desirable.

John

The presence and absence data were collected in 4 samples, and when I try to create an object with use as Yearly site covariates with the command:

seasons = matrix (c ("1", "2", "3", "4"), 19, 4, byrow = TRUE)

When I will create the object with the command:

umf = unmarkedMultFrame (y = y, siteCovs = bird.sitecov, yearlySiteCovs = list (year = seasons), numPrimary = 4)

The following message appears:
Warning message:
yearlySiteCovs contains characters. Converting them to factors.

Does anyone know how I can help to solve this problem?

I apologize if this subject has already been discussed on another topic. I hope to learn a lot from you all.

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Problem with the dynamic occupancy models script
messages.body_plain:
To add a bit more context:

In older versions of R (<4), variables that were character strings (like "seasons") were automatically converted to factors when added to a data frame. In R version 4 or greater, the R team changed this default so now characters were no longer converted to factors automatically. Unmarked still needs them to be factors, so unmarked now does the conversion itself and warns you just in case you didn't mean for it to happen.

In your analysis, is season supposed to be a categorical variable (I suspect it is)? If so leave the quotes and ignore the warning. Is season supposed to be a numeric/continuous variable? Then remove the quotes as Alistair suggests and you should no longer get a warning. Either way the model should run, but you will not get the same results both ways.

Ken

messages.subject: Problem with pcountOpen results
messages.subject_clean: Problem with pcountOpen results
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I would like to estimate a wildebeest population size from game count.
The survey comprises 12 transects which are repeated 12 times between September and October. Each transect are driven 12 times. Each individual sighted are reported.

This is an example of the table I have:
Transect Rep   Tot
 1        1     2
 1        2     0
1        3     4
1        4     6
1        5     1
1        6     0
1        7     0
1        8     0

I built a matrix with 12 rows (12 transects) and 12 columns (12 replicates)

To estimate the population size I used unmarkedFramePCO and pcountOpen:
umf <- unmarkedFramePCO(y = Wild_2020, numPrimary = 12, siteCovs = TreeCover_by_transect)

fm1_Wild <- pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~1, ~TreeCover, data = umf, K = 200)

re_Wild_1 <- ranef(fm1_Wild)
mean(colSums(bup(re_Wild_1))) # population size

But, the number that the model gave me is very high compared to the results obtained from another model (excel model). So, I am not sure that the method I used is correct.

Does anyone know how I should do it?

Thank you in advance for your help.

Anne

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Problem with the dynamic occupancy models script
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Problem with the dynamic occupancy models script
messages.body_plain:
It's hard to test without the actual data in hand, but I think the problem is with your "y". You define it as

y <- bird[,2:90]

which will result in a matrix with 89 columns ( = 89 observations per site total). However, you also say you have numPrimary = 4. There should be the same number of observations in each primary period, but right now there isn't (89/4=22.25).
unmarked is getting confused by this uneven number of obs and giving a not-very-informative error message, which should be fixed so it is more helpful.

Perhaps this is a typo in your code and it is supposed to be, say,  y = bird[,2:89] so that you have 88 total observations (88/4 = even 22 per primary period).

Or maybe you actually have a different number of observations in one of your primary periods (e.g. one year had 23 but all the others had 22). This is fine, but you have to pad out your y matrix with appropriately placed columns of NAs so that all primary periods appear to have the same number of observations.

Ken

Dear Colleagues

Apologies for cross-posting and for this non-modelling related message. Please feel free to pass this on to anyone you think might be considering a MSc and has interests in statistical ecology.

We are very pleased to announce that we are taking applications for the second intake of our new MSc in Statistical Ecology detailed in the attached leaflet. This year there are two fee-waiver scholarships available, which can be applied for when applying for admission to the MSc.

The MSc aims to give students
a sound understanding of the statistical foundations of modern methods in statistical ecology
Knowledge and skills to use these methods effectively
experience of applying them to real-world problems, under the supervision of experts, some of whom are leading researchers in this field

The Programme involves two semesters of taught courses and a 3-month summer research dissertation. It is taught by staff at the interdisciplinary Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/). The summer dissertation includes optional placements with collaborators in the UK or abroad, to give students experience of dealing with real-world problems in statistical ecology.

We are delighted to announce that we intend to award scholarships to partially or fully cover MSc fees to selected successful applicants.

More information is available here:

Tomaz

Em quinta-feira, 11 de fevereiro de 2021 às 11:36:56 UTC-4, Ken Kellner escreveu:
> It's hard to test without the actual data in hand, but I think the problem is with your "y". You define it as
>
> y <- bird[,2:90]
>
> which will result in a matrix with 89 columns ( = 89 observations per site total). However, you also say you have numPrimary = 4. There should be the same number of observations in each primary period, but right now there isn't (89/4=22.25).
> unmarked is getting confused by this uneven number of obs and giving a not-very-informative error message, which should be fixed so it is more helpful.
>
> Perhaps this is a typo in your code and it is supposed to be, say,  y = bird[,2:89] so that you have 88 total observations (88/4 = even 22 per primary period).
>
> Or maybe you actually have a different number of observations in one of your primary periods (e.g. one year had 23 but all the others had 22). This is fine, but you have to pad out your y matrix with appropriately placed columns of NAs so that all primary periods appear to have the same number of observations.
>
> Ken
>
> On Thursday, February 11, 2021 at 9:36:14 AM UTC-5 tomazram...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Thank you all for your help.

> > y <-bird [, 2: 90]
> > bird.site <-bird [, 91: 93]
> > bird.sitecov = data.frame (bird.site)
> > seasons = matrix (c ("1", "2", "3", "4"), 19, 4, byrow = TRUE)
> > umf = unmarkedMultFrame (y = y, siteCovs = bird.sitecov, yearlySiteCovs = list (year = seasons), numPrimary = 4)

messages.body_plain:
I think there potentially a few issues to deal with.

I agree with Marc that it should be newdata = na, not newdata=nd, based on your code.

unmarked's predict() returns estimates on the response scale (in this case, occupancy probability) by default. You shouldn't use the SE you get in the predict() output to make the confidence interval as you've done here, since that can result in values <0 or >1. Instead use the 'lower' and 'upper' columns that you'll also find in the output data frame. These represent the lower and upper CI bounds (95% CI by default). You can change this to some other interval by specifying the "level" argument, e.g.

predict(fm9, type='psi', newdata=na, level=0.9)

and then use the resulting lower and and upper columns as a 90% CI.

Also, if you've normalized your covariates before putting them into an unmarkedFrame, you'll need to provide newdata values to predict() that have been normalized in the same way (i.e., subtract your sequence of values by the original mean of the variable and divide by original sd). Based on your figure I am guessing you haven't done that since predicted occupancy spikes so quickly to 1.

Ken

Em sexta-feira, 12 de fevereiro de 2021 às 16:01:14 UTC-4, Ken Kellner escreveu:
> I think there potentially a few issues to deal with.
>
> I agree with Marc that it should be newdata = na, not newdata=nd, based on your code.
>
> unmarked's predict() returns estimates on the response scale (in this case, occupancy probability) by default. You shouldn't use the SE you get in the predict() output to make the confidence interval as you've done here, since that can result in values <0 or >1. Instead use the 'lower' and 'upper' columns that you'll also find in the output data frame. These represent the lower and upper CI bounds (95% CI by default). You can change this to some other interval by specifying the "level" argument, e.g.
>
> predict(fm9, type='psi', newdata=na, level=0.9)
>
> and then use the resulting lower and and upper columns as a 90% CI.
>
> Also, if you've normalized your covariates before putting them into an unmarkedFrame, you'll need to provide newdata values to predict() that have been normalized in the same way (i.e., subtract your sequence of values by the original mean of the variable and divide by original sd). Based on your figure I am guessing you haven't done that since predicted occupancy spikes so quickly to 1.
>
> Ken

> > Dear Tomaz,

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken,

sorry to jump in, just got a bit confused with a part of your answer here and want to confirm. I understand that we "... need to provide newdata values to predict() that have been normalized in the same way ...". However, usually, this scale is not very interesting to see the effect or making decisions. So, I thought it was correct to build a graph in the original scale just by providing a sequence of values in the original scale and plot it using the predicted values, is this wrong? It's probably more a visualization thing, but I´m now wondering. Should I predict() again with original values in order to do this?

Please see a commented example below in case it is useful for your feedback

Thank you very much.

Lain
----------

newData1  <-  data.frame(Tree.Cover.Cam = seq(-0.7123054, 4.6376593, by = 0.1))   #normalized using scale()
pred1 <- predict(psi_just_tree,  type  =  "state",  newdata  =  newData1,  appendData  =  TRUE)
pred1

#plot normalized data
f <- ggplot(pred1,aes(Tree.Cover.Cam, Predicted, ymin=lower,ymax=upper))
f + geom_line(colour = "blue") +
  geom_ribbon(alpha=0.2,colour=NA) +
  labs(x = "Density of trees(std)", y = "prob. occ") # graph showing that relationship with x being in the scaled covariate

# on the original scale

range(site_covs1$Tree.Cover.Cam) # 0.0-38.88 (original values of covariate)
tree.raw <- seq(0, 38.8, length= 54) # for the graph

#plot

fa <- ggplot(pred1,aes(tree.raw, Predicted, ymin=lower,ymax=upper))
fa + geom_line(colour = "blue") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x =tree.raw, ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2)+
  labs(x = "Density_tree(original)", y = " pred occ (original)") +
 theme(axis.text=element_text(size=15),axis.line=element_line(colour="black"))

On Fri, Feb 12, 2021 at 10:01 PM Ken Kellner <ken.k...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I think there potentially a few issues to deal with.
>
> I agree with Marc that it should be newdata = na, not newdata=nd, based on your code.
>
> unmarked's predict() returns estimates on the response scale (in this case, occupancy probability) by default. You shouldn't use the SE you get in the predict() output to make the confidence interval as you've done here, since that can result in values <0 or >1. Instead use the 'lower' and 'upper' columns that you'll also find in the output data frame. These represent the lower and upper CI bounds (95% CI by default). You can change this to some other interval by specifying the "level" argument, e.g.
>
> predict(fm9, type='psi', newdata=na, level=0.9)
>
> and then use the resulting lower and and upper columns as a 90% CI.
>
> Also, if you've normalized your covariates before putting them into an unmarkedFrame, you'll need to provide newdata values to predict() that have been normalized in the same way (i.e., subtract your sequence of values by the original mean of the variable and divide by original sd). Based on your figure I am guessing you haven't done that since predicted occupancy spikes so quickly to 1.
>
> Ken
> On Friday, February 12, 2021 at 2:21:56 PM UTC-5 Kery Marc wrote:
> > Dear Tomaz,
> >
> > these predictions are on a link-transformed scale, so for the CIs, you have to do plogis(Predicted +/- 1.96 * SE).
> >
> > And then, in your code, in the predict function you should have newdata = na, I would say.
> >
> > Does this help ?
> >
> > Best regards  -- Marc

Hi Lain,

I am not sure your solution is correct. You want to take 'tree.raw' as a new covariate that is used for prediction and so you choose it to cover the entire range of the observed covariate in an even way.

What you must do then is first to scale 'tree.raw' with the mean and the standard deviation that was used by scale() when you scaled the original covariate before using it in the fitted model. So, you do something like:

tree.pred <- (tree.raw - mean.original.tree.data) / sd.original.tree.data

And then you supply 'tree.pred' in the predict function. Only now can you plot the prediction against 'tree.raw'.

Best regards  --- Marc

You shouldn't use the SE you get in the predict() output to make the confidence interval as you've done here, since that can result in values <0 or >1. > Also, if you've normalized your covariates before putting them into an unmarkedFrame, you'll need to provide newdata values to predict() that have been normalized in the same way (i.e., subtract your sequence of values by the original mean of the variable and divide by original sd). messages.body_plain:
First, to your main question, I agree that in most cases you would want to plot the covariate on its original scale.

Lain, I share Marc's concern about your approach here. I think it *could* be correct, it's hard to tell just from the code you provided. The key point is: do the min and max of the scaled sequence (in your newdata) correspond to transformed versions of the min and max of the unscaled data, and are the two sequences the same length and evenly spaced? If so you are probably OK, but it's not clear from your code. For example, is length(newdata$Tree.Cover.Cam) 54 to match the length of tree.raw? This is kind of hard to sort out in words so I wrote up an example of possible ways to do it, and end with an example of the way I think you should do it.

library(unmarked)

# Simulate data
set.seed(123)
x <- runif(100,0,10)
psi <- plogis(-0.5 + 0.2 * x)
z <- rbinom(100, 1, psi)

y <- matrix(NA, nrow=100, ncol=5)
for (i in 1:100){
  y[i,] <- rbinom(5, 1, 0.5*z[i])
}

# normalize x first
mn_x <- mean(x); sd_x <- sd(x)
x_scale <- (x - mn_x)/sd_x
# Fit model
umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=x_scale))
fm1 <- occu(~1~x, umf1)

Now to predict. I'll show  two correct approaches and one incorrect approach to predicting with a scaled covariate.

# create x sequence on original scale for plot
x_seq <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out=100)

# Approach 1:
# normalize the x sequence by scaling by original mean/sd
# this is what Marc suggested
x_scale_seq1 <- (x_seq - mn_x)/sd_x
pr1 <- predict(fm1, "state", newdata=data.frame(x=x_scale_seq1))

# Approach 2:
# get a sequence between min and max of *scaled* values
# remember we generated x_scale above when making the umf
# this is what Lain did I think
x_scale_seq2 <- seq(min(x_scale), max(x_scale), length.out=100)
pr2 <- predict(fm1, "state", newdata=data.frame(x=x_scale_seq2))

# Approach 3 (INCORRECT):
# Predict directly with original, untransformed x sequence
pr_bad <- predict(fm1, "state", newdata=data.frame(x=x_seq))

Finally, I'll generate plots for each of the 3 approaches, plus a plot where we put the original X on the x-axis.

# Make plot
png("fig1.png")
par(mfrow=c(2,2))

# Plot with x sequence 1
plot(x_scale_seq1, pr1$Predicted, type="line", main="predict with\nx_scale_seq1", ylab="psi")
# Plot with x sequence 2
plot(x_scale_seq2, pr2$Predicted, type="line", main="predict with\nx_scale_seq2", ylab="psi")
# Incorrect plot
plot(x_seq, pr_bad$Predicted, type="line", ylab="psi", main="incorrect: predict\nusing original x")
# Plot with x sequence 1 but put real x on x axis
plot(x_seq, pr1$Predicted, type='line', main="predict with\nx_scale_seq1\noriginal on x-axis", ylab="psi")
dev.off()

As you can see as long as you do it correctly the two approaches are equivalent (and the incorrect approach gives a different plot).

However, there is (I think) and easier way to do this: don't scale x yourself, tell unmarked to do it by putting a call to scale() in your formula.

# Put original x in unmarked frame
umf2 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=x))

# Scale x in the formula and fit model again
fm2 <- occu(~1~scale(x), umf2)

The estimates from fm1 and fm2 will be identical. Now you can just use the original x sequence directly to predict, unmarked scales x automatically based on original mean and sd.

# Use original x_seq
pr3 <- predict(fm2, "state", newdata=data.frame(x=x_seq))

# Plot and compare with previous approach to show they are the same
png("fig2.png", width=600, height=480)
par(mfrow=c(1,2))

# our new plot
plot(x_seq, pr3$Predicted, type='line', main="using scale() in formula", ylab="psi")

# our original plot
plot(x_seq, pr2$Predicted, type="line", main="predict with\nx_scale_seq1\noriginal on x-axis",
     ylab="psi")
dev.off()

Instead use the 'lower' and 'upper' columns that you'll also find in the output data frame. These represent the lower and upper CI bounds (95% CI by default). You can change this to some other interval by specifying the "level" argument, e.g.
> >
> > predict(fm9, type='psi', newdata=na, level=0.9)
> >
> > and then use the resulting lower and and upper columns as a 90% CI.
> >
> > Also, if you've normalized your covariates before putting them into an unmarkedFrame, you'll need to provide newdata values to predict() that have been normalized in the same way (i.e., subtract your sequence of values by the original mean of the variable and divide by original sd). On Sat, Feb 13, 2021 at 4:08 PM Ken Kellner <ken.k...@gmail.com> wrote:

> First, to your main question, I agree that in most cases you would want to plot the covariate on its original scale.
>
> Lain, I share Marc's concern about your approach here. I think it *could* be correct, it's hard to tell just from the code you provided. The key point is: do the min and max of the scaled sequence (in your newdata) correspond to transformed versions of the min and max of the unscaled data, and are the two sequences the same length and evenly spaced? If so you are probably OK, but it's not clear from your code. For example, is length(newdata$Tree.Cover.Cam) 54 to match the length of tree.raw? This is kind of hard to sort out in words so I wrote up an example of possible ways to do it, and end with an example of the way I think you should do it.
>
> library(unmarked)
>
> # Simulate data
> set.seed(123)
> x <- runif(100,0,10)
> psi <- plogis(-0.5 + 0.2 * x)
> z <- rbinom(100, 1, psi)
>
> y <- matrix(NA, nrow=100, ncol=5)
> for (i in 1:100){
>   y[i,] <- rbinom(5, 1, 0.5*z[i])
> }
>
> # normalize x first
> mn_x <- mean(x); sd_x <- sd(x)
> x_scale <- (x - mn_x)/sd_x
> # Fit model
> umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=x_scale))
> fm1 <- occu(~1~x, umf1)
>
> Now to predict. I'll show  two correct approaches and one incorrect approach to predicting with a scaled covariate.
>
> # create x sequence on original scale for plot
> x_seq <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out=100)
>
> # Approach 1:
> # normalize the x sequence by scaling by original mean/sd
> # this is what Marc suggested
> x_scale_seq1 <- (x_seq - mn_x)/sd_x
> pr1 <- predict(fm1, "state", newdata=data.frame(x=x_scale_seq1))
>
> # Approach 2:
> # get a sequence between min and max of *scaled* values
> # remember we generated x_scale above when making the umf
> # this is what Lain did I think
> x_scale_seq2 <- seq(min(x_scale), max(x_scale), length.out=100)
> pr2 <- predict(fm1, "state", newdata=data.frame(x=x_scale_seq2))
>
> # Approach 3 (INCORRECT):
> # Predict directly with original, untransformed x sequence
> pr_bad <- predict(fm1, "state", newdata=data.frame(x=x_seq))
>
> Finally, I'll generate plots for each of the 3 approaches, plus a plot where we put the original X on the x-axis.
>
> # Make plot
> png("fig1.png")
> par(mfrow=c(2,2))
>
> # Plot with x sequence 1
> plot(x_scale_seq1, pr1$Predicted, type="line", main="predict with\nx_scale_seq1", ylab="psi")
> # Plot with x sequence 2
> plot(x_scale_seq2, pr2$Predicted, type="line", main="predict with\nx_scale_seq2", ylab="psi")
> # Incorrect plot
> plot(x_seq, pr_bad$Predicted, type="line", ylab="psi", main="incorrect: predict\nusing original x")
> # Plot with x sequence 1 but put real x on x axis
> plot(x_seq, pr1$Predicted, type='line', main="predict with\nx_scale_seq1\noriginal on x-axis", ylab="psi")
> dev.off()
>
> As you can see as long as you do it correctly the two approaches are equivalent (and the incorrect approach gives a different plot).
>
> However, there is (I think) and easier way to do this: don't scale x yourself, tell unmarked to do it by putting a call to scale() in your formula.
>
> # Put original x in unmarked frame
> umf2 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=x))
>
> # Scale x in the formula and fit model again
> fm2 <- occu(~1~scale(x), umf2)
>
> The estimates from fm1 and fm2 will be identical. Now you can just use the original x sequence directly to predict, unmarked scales x automatically based on original mean and sd.
>
> # Use original x_seq
> pr3 <- predict(fm2, "state", newdata=data.frame(x=x_seq))
>
> # Plot and compare with previous approach to show they are the same
> png("fig2.png", width=600, height=480)
> par(mfrow=c(1,2))
>
> # our new plot
> plot(x_seq, pr3$Predicted, type='line', main="using scale() in formula", ylab="psi")
>
> # our original plot
> plot(x_seq, pr2$Predicted, type="line", main="predict with\nx_scale_seq1\noriginal on x-axis",
>      ylab="psi")
> dev.off()
>
>

messages.subject: Preliminary questions on N-mixture models
messages.subject_clean: Preliminary questions on N-mixture models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm a MS student interested in using N-mixture modelling to estimate abundance from a count dataset I've collected. I've only just started exploring them and have some beginner conceptual questions.

First, do these models assume that surveyed sites are occupied? My survey methods have a high detection probability as estimated from static occupancy modeling ( ~0.7) but I have several sites with zero detections across all their respective repeated surveys. However, when examining output from N-mixture models I fit using pcount(), I still get low abundance estimates from sites with zero detections. Due to the sites with all zeros, would fitting models using a ZIP mixture be reasonable?

Additionally, the detection probabilities given by N-mixture models are much lower than those given by occupancy models. Do detection probabilities for N-mixture denote detectability of the species, as in occupancy models, or do they describe detection probability of detecting an individual?

Finally, I have ran into what I'm learning is a common issue: the "good fit, bad estimate" problem. NB mixture models I fit have the lowest AICc and have a more reasonable goodness of fit compared to ZIP and P models (c-hat is around 1 for my NB global model but >2 for both ZIP and P). However, all NB estimates are sensitive to K, unlike ZIP and P models. Given this situation, what following steps would be recommended? I have thought of selecting P or ZIP models using QAICc to account for overdispersion these provide, while retaining the finite estimates. Would I be on the right track there?

Thank you for any help or information,

David Rosenbaum

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Preliminary questions on N-mixture models
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Preliminary questions on N-mixture models
messages.body_plain:
A few quick thoughts:
The "true" abundance is modeled with a Poisson (or Negative Binomial, or something similar) distribution. Those distributions do allow for 0's, so the models aren't exactly assuming that the sites are occupied. What they're giving you is an estimate of the abundance/density at the sites. That estimate comes from the mean of a Poisson (or other) distribution, and when you have observations at some sites, the mean of the distribution will never be exactly 0. It might be very low, but not 0.
The detection probabilities are different. In occupancy models the detection probability is the probability of detecting a species if it is present. In N-mixture models, the detection probability is the probability of detecting any given individual that is present.
This one's a bit tougher. N-mixture models can be quite sensitive to some of the modeling assumptions, and when you're working with real-world data it can be difficult to know when a model is leading you astray. I would be inclined to trust the NB a little more than the P model because the NB can account for overdispersion in counts. K is really a nuisance parameter. Theoretically it should be infiniti, but we set it lower for computational reasons. One approach is to just keep making K larger until estimates stabilize. Another approach that you could take would be to fit the models using the UBMS package <https://kenkellner.com/ubms/>, which allows you to easily add random effects to the model (I think - I haven't actually used UBMS myself). Adding random effects will help to account for overdispersion beyond what the NB can account for (e.g. overdispersion in detection probability). Fitting models in a Bayesian framework with the UBMS package also has the benefit of assessing the models in more of a simulation framework (i.e. comparing the data that you observed to data simulated from the model fit - ideally they will look very similar). You can do the same thing in a frequentist framework, too, it's just less commonly done.
Philip Shirk
Postdoctoral Scholar
Cooperative Institute of Marine Resources Studies
Oregon State University

However, all NB estimates are sensitive to K, unlike ZIP and P models. Given this situation, what following steps would be recommended? I have thought of selecting P or ZIP models using QAICc to account for overdispersion these provide, while retaining the finite estimates. Would I be on the right track there?

>

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Size of the reserve considered
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Size of the reserve considered
messages.body_plain:
The model gives estimates of abundance (or density) per sample unit. The definition of sample unit isn't always clear. If your samples came from a defined sample area (e.g. 20 m radius), then you can extrapolate from the sample area to the study area. If your sample area is undefined (e.g. you recorded every animal you could detect, but it's unclear how large an area that is), then it's harder to get a precise estimate of the population size over the whole reserve. You could guess what your sample area is (probably make 3 guesses: the minimum, best guess, and maximum areas you think realistic) and make extrapolations based on each of them. Also keep in mind that if you have habitat covariates on the abundance estimates that you'll need to account for those habitat covariates across the entire reserve. (If you have a map of covariate values across the reserve, you could create a grid with boxes equal in size to your estimated sample area. Then estimate the abundance in each of those grid cells and add them together.)

Philip Shirk
Postdoctoral Scholar
Cooperative Institute of Marine Resources Studies
Oregon State University

messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip,

Thank you for the insight! I have tried adjusting K (even up to 1,000,000!) for my NB models but the estimates never stabilize and become quite unreasonable when K is this high. I will do some research on UBMS.

David Rosenbaum

On Mon, Feb 15, 2021 at 1:03 PM Philip Shirk <philip...@gmail.com> wrote:

> A few quick thoughts:
> The "true" abundance is modeled with a Poisson (or Negative Binomial, or something similar) distribution. Those distributions do allow for 0's, so the models aren't exactly assuming that the sites are occupied. What they're giving you is an estimate of the abundance/density at the sites. That estimate comes from the mean of a Poisson (or other) distribution, and when you have observations at some sites, the mean of the distribution will never be exactly 0. It might be very low, but not 0.
> The detection probabilities are different. In occupancy models the detection probability is the probability of detecting a species if it is present. In N-mixture models, the detection probability is the probability of detecting any given individual that is present.
> This one's a bit tougher. N-mixture models can be quite sensitive to some of the modeling assumptions, and when you're working with real-world data it can be difficult to know when a model is leading you astray. I would be inclined to trust the NB a little more than the P model because the NB can account for overdispersion in counts. K is really a nuisance parameter. Theoretically it should be infiniti, but we set it lower for computational reasons. One approach is to just keep making K larger until estimates stabilize. Another approach that you could take would be to fit the models using the UBMS package <https://kenkellner.com/ubms/>, which allows you to easily add random effects to the model (I think - I haven't actually used UBMS myself). Adding random effects will help to account for overdispersion beyond what the NB can account for (e.g. overdispersion in detection probability). Fitting models in a Bayesian framework with the UBMS package also has the benefit of assessing the models in more of a simulation framework (i.e. comparing the data that you observed to data simulated from the model fit - ideally they will look very similar). You can do the same thing in a frequentist framework, too, it's just less commonly done.
> Philip Shirk
> Postdoctoral Scholar
> Cooperative Institute of Marine Resources Studies
> Oregon State University
>
>
> On Mon, Feb 15, 2021 at 9:12 AM david rosenbaum <rsnb...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I'm a MS student interested in using N-mixture modelling to estimate abundance from a count dataset I've collected. I've only just started exploring them and have some beginner conceptual questions.
> >
> > First, do these models assume that surveyed sites are occupied? My survey methods have a high detection probability as estimated from static occupancy modeling ( ~0.7) but I have several sites with zero detections across all their respective repeated surveys. However, when examining output from N-mixture models I fit using pcount(), I still get low abundance estimates from sites with zero detections. Due to the sites with all zeros, would fitting models using a ZIP mixture be reasonable?
> >
> > Additionally, the detection probabilities given by N-mixture models are much lower than those given by occupancy models. Do detection probabilities for N-mixture denote detectability of the species, as in occupancy models, or do they describe detection probability of detecting an individual?
> >
> > Finally, I have ran into what I'm learning is a common issue: the "good fit, bad estimate" problem. NB mixture models I fit have the lowest AICc and have a more reasonable goodness of fit compared to ZIP and P models (c-hat is around 1 for my NB global model but >2 for both ZIP and P). However, all NB estimates are sensitive to K, unlike ZIP and P models. Given this situation, what following steps would be recommended? I have thought of selecting P or ZIP models using QAICc to account for overdispersion these provide, while retaining the finite estimates. Would I be on the right track there?
> >
> > Thank you for any help or information,
> >
> > David Rosenbaum
> >

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Size of the reserve considered
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Size of the reserve considered
messages.body_plain:
Start by converting the estimated density from individuals per sample plots to individuals per hectare. Then, ignoring the habitat covariate, that would also be your estimate of density for the whole reserve. You could multiply the density by the reserve area to get the total number of individuals in the reserve. But with the habitat covariate, you want to split up the reserve into a bunch of little boxes that each the same size as your sample areas. So if your reserve is 100 ha and each sample area is 1 ha, you would have 100 boxes. Get the average tree cover in each of those boxes and use the fit model to predict the density in each of the 100 boxes. (All boxes that have the same habitat will have the same predicted density.) Once you have those, you can just add together the number of organisms in all the boxes to get the total number in the reserve. The transect replicates that you have are necessary for fitting the original model, but not for extrapolating the results.

Philip Shirk

> > Le 17 févr. 2021 à 07:11, Philip Shirk <fil...@gmail.com> a écrit :
> >
> > Start by converting the estimated density from individuals per sample plots to individuals per hectare. Then, ignoring the habitat covariate, that would also be your estimate of density for the whole reserve. You could multiply the density by the reserve area to get the total number of individuals in the reserve. But with the habitat covariate, you want to split up the reserve into a bunch of little boxes that each the same size as your sample areas. So if your reserve is 100 ha and each sample area is 1 ha, you would have 100 boxes. Get the average tree cover in each of those boxes and use the fit model to predict the density in each of the 100 boxes. (All boxes that have the same habitat will have the same predicted density.) Once you have those, you can just add together the number of organisms in all the boxes to get the total number in the reserve. The transect replicates that you have are necessary for fitting the original model, but not for extrapolating the results.

> > > >
> > > > The model gives estimates of abundance (or density) per sample unit. The definition of sample unit isn't always clear. If your samples came from a defined sample area (e.g. 20 m radius), then you can extrapolate from the sample area to the study area. If your sample area is undefined (e.g. you recorded every animal you could detect, but it's unclear how large an area that is), then it's harder to get a precise estimate of the population size over the whole reserve. You could guess what your sample area is (probably make 3 guesses: the minimum, best guess, and maximum areas you think realistic) and make extrapolations based on each of them. Also keep in mind that if you have habitat covariates on the abundance estimates that you'll need to account for those habitat covariates across the entire reserve. (If you have a map of covariate values across the reserve, you could create a grid with boxes equal in size to your estimated sample area. Then estimate the abundance in each of those grid cells and add them together.)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vishnu,

Use the 'projected' values if you want predictions of the *expected* value of occupancy. These are based on the maximum likelihood estimates and the formula:

PrOccupied(i,t) = PrOccupied(i,t-1)*[1-PrExtinction(i,t-1)] + [1-PrOccupied(i,t-1)]*PrColonized(i,t-1)

Use the 'smoothed' values if you want predictions of the *realized* value of the latent occupancy state, conditional on the entire sequence of observations. These smoothed values are computed using the forward-backward algorithm:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward%E2%80%93backward_algorithm

In other words, use the smoothed values if you want estimates of occupancy at the specific sites you sampled during the specific time period when you sampled. Use the projected values if you want standard predictions that might be useful for assessing what would happen if you repeated the study under similar conditions.

A great early reference on hidden Markov models and smoothing, in the context of occupancy models, is:

Fiske, I.J., Royle, J.A. and Gross, K., 2014. Inference for finite-sample trajectories in dynamic multi-state site-occupancy models using hidden Markov model smoothing. Environmental and ecological statistics, 21(2), pp.313-328.

Richard

On Thursday, February 25, 2021 at 1:04:35 AM UTC+11 rchandler wrote:
> Hi Vishnu,
>
> Use the 'projected' values if you want predictions of the *expected* value of occupancy. These are based on the maximum likelihood estimates and the formula:
>
> PrOccupied(i,t) = PrOccupied(i,t-1)*[1-PrExtinction(i,t-1)] + [1-PrOccupied(i,t-1)]*PrColonized(i,t-1)
>
> Use the 'smoothed' values if you want predictions of the *realized* value of the latent occupancy state, conditional on the entire sequence of observations. These smoothed values are computed using the forward-backward algorithm:
>
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward%E2%80%93backward_algorithm
>
> In other words, use the smoothed values if you want estimates of occupancy at the specific sites you sampled during the specific time period when you sampled. Use the projected values if you want standard predictions that might be useful for assessing what would happen if you repeated the study under similar conditions.
>
> A great early reference on hidden Markov models and smoothing, in the context of occupancy models, is:

Hi Vishnu,

In that case, you can use `predict` to give you estimates, SEs, and CIs for initial occupancy in the baited and unbaited sites. See the examples here:

help(unmarked)

The predictions will just be:

Pr(occupied at t=1 at baited site) = plogis(-1.46)
Pr(occupied at t=1 at unbaited site) = plogis(-1.46+0.65)

Richard

methods to estimate population parameters, with emphasis on the

information, a glimpse of the program, and the link to the registration
platform on the EURING 2021 web site:

Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Two questions here:

1) I think this might be a pretty basic question, but I haven't been able to find the answer (in a way that I could pick out the answer) either in the unmarked PDF or here in this group. I'm working on creating a multi-season model with camera trap data using the colext function. I have four years of data. The first year has data from 60 cameras. Subsequent years have data from 41-43 cameras, but it's not the all the same cameras "missing" from each year (some cameras went down for a year and then came back up, while others were taken down and stayed down).

If I want to consider all four years of data, can I use all the sites that reach my threshold for number of days in a season? Or do I need to cut down and only use cameras that have sufficient data for each year that I'd like to consider?

2) My second question relates to the cameraOperation function in camtrap to make my unmarkedMultFrame object. For multi-year work, do I need to use sessionCol in the cameraOperation function? Right now I have data in a format that has a single row for every camera, representing the duration of their operational time (with down time included as problems). Should that be alright? I recognize this isn't specifically a question about unmarked and I've already posted it in the camtrap Google group--please ignore if inappropriate here.

Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
Vishnu,

If I'm understanding you correctly what you ultimately want is a matrix of occupancy with two rows (one for baited and one for unbaited) and two columns (one for season 1 and one for season 2). If that's correct I think posterior prediction with Empirical Bayes is a solution. Rather than explain here see this previous thread:

https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/l9CCdAplmAo/m/H9r42ErIBAAJ

The code in that thread is outdated since this feature is now officially part of unmarked. I wrote up a quick example below using the built-in frogs dataset which should get you started. See also ?predict, specifically the final section in the help file related to unmarkedRanef objects.

Ken

-------------------------------

library(unmarked)

data(frogs)
umf <- formatMult(masspcru)[1:200,]

# Make fake categorical covariate "x" with two levels a and b
set.seed(123)
siteCovs(umf) <- data.frame(x = factor(sample(letters[1:2],numSites(umf), replace=T)))
head(siteCovs(umf))

# Fit model with effect of x on initial occupancy
(fit <- colext(~x, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf))

# Get estimates of latent occupancy state (z) at each site using empirical bayes
r <- ranef(fit)

# Now we can generate an empirical bayes posterior predictive distribution
# for mean occupancy in each group a and b

# Function that takes argument zmat, which will be a matrix M x T of latent occupancy
# zmat will be 200 x 7 in this case since there are 200 sites and 7 primary periods
split_z_by_x <- function(zmat){
  T <- ncol(zmat) # primary periods
  x <- siteCovs(umf)$x
  z_a <- zmat[x=="a",] # sites where x == "a"
  z_b <- zmat[x=="b",] # sites where x == "b"
  #output object: 2 rows (for categories a and b) and 7 columns (for 7 primary periods)
  out <- matrix(NA, nrow=2, ncol=T)
  out[1,] <- colMeans(z_a) # mean of posterior of z for sites with x == "a"
  out[2,] <- colMeans(z_b) # same for b
  rownames(out) <- c("a","b")
  colnames(out) <- 1:T
  out
}

# Use predict method for unmarkedRanef, supplying the function, and get 100 samples
pr <- predict(r, func=split_z_by_x, nsim=100)

# Output will be 2 groups x 7 periods x 100 simulations
dim(pr)

#Get mean of posterior for each group and primary period
(post_mean <- apply(pr, c(1,2), mean))

# Get 95% CI for each group and primary period
post_ci <- apply(pr, c(1,2), quantile, c(0.025,0.975))

# Plot means and 95% CIs
plot(x=1:7-0.1, y=post_mean[1,], col='blue', type='b', ylim=c(0.82,1),
    ylab="Proportion occupied", xlab="Primary period")
for (i in 1:7){
  segments(i-0.1, post_ci[1,1,i], i-0.1, post_ci[2,1,i], col='blue')
}

lines(1:7+0.1, post_mean[2,], type='b', col='red')
for (i in 1:7){
  segments(i+0.1, post_ci[1,2,i], i+0.1, post_ci[2,2,i], col='red')
}

legend("bottomright", col=c("blue","red"), legend=c("a","b"),pch=21,
       title="Value of x")
